title: Jeremiah 26:17–24
context: Certain elders of the land speak to the assembly, recalling that Micah the Morashtite prophesied in Hezekiah’s day that “Zion will be plowed as a field” (quoting Mic 3:12), and that Hezekiah did not kill him but feared the LORD, “and the LORD relented of the disaster.” The narrator then tells of Uriah the son of Shemaiah, who prophesied the same message, fled to Egypt, and was brought back and killed by Jehoiakim, and closes by saying that “the hand of Ahikam the son of Shaphan was with Jeremiah,” so that he was not handed over to death. Both traditions share the ground that faithful prophets may be protected or may die, that God remains faithful in both, and that the relenting language points to the existing boxes at 1 Samuel 15:29 and Jonah 3:10.

verses.text: Then certain of the elders of the land rose up, and spoke to all the assembly of the people, saying,
verses.arminianNotes:
“Then certain of the elders of the land rose up, and spoke to all the assembly of the people.” Arminian readers note that elders appeal to history.

Their voice adds weight to the princes’ verdict.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see God raising up voices of wisdom at a critical moment.

Shared ground: both traditions read the elders as speakers who use Israel’s memory of earlier prophets to guide the present decision.

verses.text: “Micah the Morashtite prophesied in the days of Hezekiah king of Judah; and he spoke to all the people of Judah, saying, ‘The LORD of Armies says: “ ‘Zion will be plowed as a field, and Jerusalem will become heaps, and the mountain of the house as the high places of a forest.’
verses.arminianNotes:
The elders recall that “Micah the Morashtite prophesied in the days of Hezekiah king of Judah,” saying that “Zion will be plowed as a field.” Arminian readers note that this quotes Mic 3:12.

An earlier prophet had spoken similar words and was spared.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see the elders appealing to Scripture already known among them.

Shared ground: both traditions agree that Micah’s precedent shows judgment oracles can be warnings meant to lead to repentance.

verses.text: Did Hezekiah king of Judah and all Judah put him to death? Didn’t he fear the LORD, and entreat the favor of the LORD, and the LORD relented of the disaster which he had pronounced against them? We would commit great evil against our own souls that way!”
verses.arminianNotes:
The elders ask, “Didn’t he fear the LORD, and entreat the favor of the LORD, and the LORD relented of the disaster which he had pronounced against them?” Arminian readers see God responding to Hezekiah’s repentance.

They point to 1 Samuel 15:29 and Jonah 3:10.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers read the relenting within God’s eternal counsel, which includes the means of repentance, pointing to the same boxes.

Shared ground: both traditions agree the elders’ warning is sound: “We would commit great evil against our own souls that way.”

verses.text: There was also a man who prophesied in the LORD’s name, Uriah the son of Shemaiah of Kiriath Jearim; and he prophesied against this city and against this land according to all the words of Jeremiah.
verses.arminianNotes:
“There was also a man who prophesied in the LORD’s name, Uriah the son of Shemaiah of Kiriath Jearim.” Arminian readers note that Uriah preached “according to all the words of Jeremiah.”

The narrator introduces a second, sadder example.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see another faithful witness to the same message.

Shared ground: both traditions read Uriah as a true prophet whose story stands beside Micah’s as a sober contrast.

verses.text: When Jehoiakim the king, with all his mighty men and all the princes heard his words, the king sought to put him to death; but when Uriah heard it, he was afraid, and fled, and went into Egypt.
verses.arminianNotes:
“When Jehoiakim the king, with all his mighty men and all the princes heard his words, the king sought to put him to death; but when Uriah heard it, he was afraid, and fled.” Arminian readers note Uriah’s fear.

They do not condemn his flight.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise read his fear with compassion rather than judgment.

Shared ground: both traditions note that the text does not evaluate Uriah’s flight, and both avoid adding motives the narrator does not give.

verses.text: Then Jehoiakim the king sent Elnathan the son of Achbor and certain men with him into Egypt.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Then Jehoiakim the king sent Elnathan the son of Achbor and certain men with him into Egypt.” Arminian readers note the king’s determination to pursue the prophet.

An Elnathan son of Achbor appears again in 36:12, 25.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see the reach of royal hostility to God’s word.

Shared ground: both traditions note the later mention of Elnathan without drawing firm conclusions about his character from this verse alone.

verses.text: They fetched Uriah out of Egypt and brought him to Jehoiakim the king, who killed him with the sword and cast his dead body into the graves of the common people.
verses.arminianNotes:
“They fetched Uriah out of Egypt and brought him to Jehoiakim the king, who killed him with the sword.” Arminian readers read Uriah’s death soberly.

His body was cast “into the graves of the common people,” a mark of dishonor.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise treat the death with gravity and sorrow.

Shared ground: both traditions agree that faithful witnesses are not always delivered from death, and that Uriah’s faithfulness is not diminished by his end (cf. Heb 11:36–38).

verses.text: But the hand of Ahikam the son of Shaphan was with Jeremiah, so that they didn’t give him into the hand of the people to put him to death.
verses.arminianNotes:
“But the hand of Ahikam the son of Shaphan was with Jeremiah, so that they didn’t give him into the hand of the people to put him to death.” Arminian readers note Ahikam’s protection.

An Ahikam son of Shaphan also appears in 2 Kgs 22:12; identifying the two is likely but not stated.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see God’s providence working through a human protector.

Shared ground: both traditions read the verse plainly as Jeremiah’s preservation, while noting that Uriah was not spared, and both affirm God’s faithfulness in each case.
